result.summary: The poet invokes the Muse to sing of Aphrodite's power over gods, men and beasts, and names the three goddesses she cannot sway: Athene, Artemis and Hestia. Zeus, mocked by her power over him, makes Aphrodite desire the mortal Anchises. She adorns herself at Paphos, goes to Ida, and appears to Anchises as a maiden, and he prays to her.

scenes.title: Aphrodite's power and its limits
scenes.summary: The poet praises Aphrodite's sway over all living things, then names Athene, Artemis and Hestia as the three she cannot move. Hestia's vow of virginity earns her honour from Zeus.

scenes.title: Zeus's plan against Aphrodite
scenes.summary: Aphrodite leads even Zeus astray into affairs with mortal women. Zeus therefore makes her desire a mortal man so she cannot mock the gods.
scenes.stakes: Zeus risks being mocked by Aphrodite among the gods.

scenes.title: Aphrodite adorns herself at Paphos
scenes.summary: Seized with desire for Anchises, Aphrodite goes to her temple at Paphos, is bathed by the Graces and dressed, then flies toward Troy.

scenes.title: Aphrodite meets Anchises on Ida
scenes.summary: Beasts follow Aphrodite and mate on Ida. She finds Anchises alone playing the lyre, appearing as a maiden. He takes her for a goddess and prays for fame and offspring.
scenes.stakes: Anchises is unknowingly in the presence of a goddess and is about to be drawn into her desire.

Epithet for her association with Cyprus.

notable_quotes.reason: Opens the list of the three goddesses Aphrodite cannot sway.
Anchises' ironic prayer for a long, prosperous life, spoken to the goddess he will lie with.

analysis.text: Aphrodite's power is universal but has limits; the hymn sets this up before showing Zeus turning her power back on herself.
The hymn explains the Trojan hero Anchises' lineage, linking Aphrodite to Aeneas, important to later Roman tradition.

legacy.text: Anchises' union with Aphrodite, producing Aeneas, was reworked by Virgil in the Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: The bracketed numbers in the text, like 2524, are page markers from the print edition, not part of the poem.

language_notes.text: Cytherea is a title of Aphrodite, from the island of Cythera, linked to her cult; "the Cyprian" refers to Cyprus, where she came ashore.
The aegis is a goatskin shield or cloak associated with Zeus and Athene, signifying protective and terrifying power.
The stray number "2524" is a footnote marker from the source edition, not part of the poem. Hestia was first swallowed and last disgorged by Cronos, hence eldest and youngest.
Touching Zeus's head was a gesture of solemn oath-taking; "sware" is archaic for "swore".
"Has her place in the midst of the house" refers to the hearth, the household's central point, where Hestia was honoured.
Hera is called Zeus's sister because both are children of Cronos and Rhea; "mates him" means she causes him to unite with mortal women.
"Sons of death" means mortal sons, born to die though their fathers are deathless gods.
"He" is Zeus, who in the preceding lines put desire for a mortal into Aphrodite's heart; the pronoun has no antecedent in this extract.
"Put to the glittering doors" means she shut them behind her.
"Coombes" are short, deep wooded valleys or hollows on a hillside.
"Neat-built" means well-constructed; the shelters are the herdsmen's huts or folds.
Anchises lists goddesses: Artemis (huntress), Leto (her mother), Themis (goddess of divine order), Athene (the Greek Athena). He pointedly names Aphrodite among them without knowing it is she.
Those who inhabit the mountain and springs are nymphs, minor female nature spirits.

context_notes.text: Athene was goddess of war strategy and of crafts such as weaving and metalwork, which is why she is linked with chariots and women's skills.
Artemis was the virgin goddess of hunting and wild places, twin sister of Apollo.
Hestia was goddess of the hearth, whose fire stood at the centre of every home and temple.
Paphos on Cyprus was a chief centre of Aphrodite's worship, with a famous sanctuary of the goddess.
The Graces were attendants of Aphrodite, goddesses of charm and beauty.
The lyre was the herdsman's and gentleman's instrument; Anchises is of the royal Trojan line, so playing it suits him.

literary_notes.text: Naming the three exceptions at once sets up the catalogue that follows and the larger theme of Aphrodite's reach and limits.
Zeus, supreme and wise, is made a fool by desire, and Hera is kept unaware; the strongest god is shown subject to Aphrodite.
Turnabout and mockery: Zeus fears Aphrodite's laughter, so he repays her with the same fate she inflicts on the gods, setting up the Anchises story.
"Many-fountained" Ida is a stock descriptive epithet, repeated in sentence 19 and typical of epic style.
The goddess who inspires desire in all creatures is herself overcome by it; the beasts' mating mirrors her own passion.
The audience knows she is a goddess in disguise, while Anchises sees only a maiden, so his reaction is shaped by the reader's greater knowledge.
The garment's shimmer is compared to the moon, conveying divine radiance.
By naming Aphrodite among possible goddesses, Anchises unknowingly guesses the truth while rejecting it.
